issues.body: The new rustdoc says everything outside the equality scope has no N3 counterpart and that an unsupported construct on a permission "merely produces no grant." That is false for collection-valued targets/assignees: `odrl-d.n3` joins target and assignee by exact IRI, so a permission naming a PartyCollection or AssetCollection can grant a request naming that same collection IRI. Only the Rust oracle's membership expansion lacks an N3 counterpart. The corrected SKILL explicitly documents this exception, so the purported cross-crate oracle contract now contradicts it.
issues.fix_hint: Replace the blanket permission statement with the same split used in the SKILL: unsupported permission constraints and `odrl:use` produce no grant, while collection-valued target/assignee fields retain exact-IRI matching but lack membership expansion. Keep the existing prohibition and unconditional-refusal rules distinct.
issues.title: Oracle rustdoc still claims every out-of-scope permission is inert

issues.body: The landed-state section says an out-of-scope construct on a permission yields no grant. As written, that covers structural collection membership, which the same PR's SKILL correctly identifies as an exact-match subset rather than an inert permission. Since this section is meant to reconcile the design with what actually landed, the blanket wording materially misstates the implemented envelope.
issues.fix_hint: Narrow the no-grant statement to unsupported constraints and `odrl:use`, then add a concise exact-IRI-only exception for PartyCollection/AssetCollection targets and assignees whose membership expansion is Rust-only.
issues.title: Landed-state reconciliation repeats the false blanket permission behavior

verdict.summary: The SKILL now correctly distinguishes exact-IRI collection matches from missing collection-membership expansion, resolving the prior finding there. However, the newly added oracle rustdoc and landed-state design text repeat the same overbroad rule-kind claim: they say everything outside the narrow equivalence scope (or any out-of-scope construct) on a permission produces no grant. Collection-valued target/assignee structure is outside exact equivalence, yet the N3 rules can still grant when the request names the collection IRI exactly; only member expansion is absent. Because these texts are presented as the cross-crate contract and design reconciliation, the caller-facing contract remains materially false. This is materially the same major finding as round 2, so progress is stagnant.
